summary: The developer machine has the core runtime, the DocumentDB MCP server and many domain skills installed, so a builder can start the Node.js + LangChain sample now and verify work against the live cluster. Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated (they described Cosmos DB databaseAccounts / RU model, or older connection formats). Missing developer choices remain (LLM provider and env vars, taxonomy, sample-data seed shape), and a few helpful CLIs (mongosh) and IaC tools are not installed but are not blockers.
summary_points: Core prerequisites are present: Node 24, npm/npx, docker, az signed-in, documentdb MCP server (data-plane) and the DocumentDB domain skills — the build can start.

Several cold answers conflated Azure DocumentDB (managed, vCore mongoClusters) with Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (RU) — resource type, CLI group, provisioning model and connection-host/port details are the main confusions.

Vector and hybrid-search features are supported and documented (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN and $search + cosmosSearch hybrid), but the cold answers used imprecise index syntax — use the documented createSearchIndexes / cosmosSearchOptions forms.
Missing but non-blocking items: explicit taxonomy, LLM/provider env vars, seed dataset, and a decision how the agent is triggered (HTTP endpoint vs CLI).
Useful developer tools absent (mongosh) or not on PATH; add them to speed interactive validation but they are not required to build the sample.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources include databases, collections etc.).
confusions.grounded_answer: The current managed DocumentDB (vCore / MongoDB-compatible clusters) resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2026-06-01 (deployment-language-arm-template)
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace 'Microsoft.DocumentDB' and historical naming where Cosmos DB used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the model answered the older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' pattern instead of the newer mongoClusters resource.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts) docs (example of the older resource)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts/mongo 'account' samples or ARM/Bicep that target databaseAccounts, they would attempt to manage the wrong resource type (Cosmos-style account) when they meant to inspect or reference the vCore mongoClusters resource; deployment templates would fail or deploy the wrong service.
improvements: Update quickstarts and the agent skill descriptions to call out 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' as the vCore-managed cluster resource and mark 'databaseAccounts' as the Cosmos DB (RU) account resource.
Add a short deprecation / distinction note to any 'databaseAccounts' docs that discuss MongoDB API to avoid conflating the two resource types.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (part of core az CLI). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=uksouth --default-consistency-level Session
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed Mongo clusters you use the az documentdb (or az cosmosdb mongocluster) command subgroup: az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show (these commands are available in the core Azure CLI command groups for DocumentDB/mongocluster management).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI docs)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The az cosmosdb create --kind MongoDB flow is how you create Cosmos DB databaseAccounts with the MongoDB API (RUs). The newer vCore-managed service lives under az documentdb mongocluster commands (or aliased az cosmosdb mongocluster in some CLI views).
confusions.build_risk: A builder who follows the cold answer would attempt to use az cosmosdb create --kind MongoDB to create a databaseAccount (RU model) rather than the intended vCore mongoClusters resource; that mis-targeting would produce the wrong provisioning model and incompatible billing and connection semantics.
improvements: Document a short CLI mapping in agent kit docs: 'For vCore clusters use az documentdb mongocluster create; az cosmosdb create --kind MongoDB creates a RU-based Cosmos DB account (different product).' Provide examples in the deployment skill.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { ... kind = "MongoDB" }
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore-managed clusters deploy as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in Bicep/ARM and Terraform (examples use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters or AzAPI/azurerm AVM modules for the mongoClusters type). The terraform azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource is for Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (RU model) and not the vCore mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM/Terraform examples)
Terraform example: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (AzAPI)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older and RU-based Cosmos DB resource uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts / azurerm_cosmosdb_account; the new vCore offering uses a distinct resource type mongoClusters — the names and provider namespace overlap and cause confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account templates would create RU-based Cosmos DB accounts, not vCore mongoClusters; the builder could provision the wrong resource or fail to deploy features (vCore tiers, DiskANN, HNSW, M30 tiers).
improvements: Add explicit examples for both models in agent kit deployment skill and call out the difference: Bicep/Terraform snippets for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters vs Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
Add a short 'which resource to use' table to documentdb-azure-deployment skill.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string for Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB MongoDB API): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false (or SRV form mongodb+srv://<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com). TLS port 10255, host suffix *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, ssl=true required.
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters the documented SRV host suffix is <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and the cluster uses SRV-compatible mongodb+srv:// URIs. The cluster node ports start at 10260 (TLS) and may enumerate per-node; typical connection strings in docs use mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256&retryWrites=false (port 10260, SRV-based discovery). The earlier cosmos.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 pattern belongs to Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (older RU account patterns) and is not the vCore cluster host/port shape.

grounding_links.title: Troubleshoot common issues in Azure DocumentDB (connection examples, port 10260)
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB (ports starting at 10260, SRV behavior)
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js (connection string example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the connection shape used by Cosmos DB's older MongoDB compatibility accounts (host suffix and port 10255). The new vCore DocumentDB clusters use the mongocluster host naming and ports starting at 10260; SRV records are used for driver discovery.

confusion_sources.title: Example Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection string docs (old model)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port would fail driver connections (DNS/port mismatch) or require incorrect TLS/option flags; developers could hard-code an invalid host and block testing.
improvements: Add a short 'connection string examples' snippet in the documentdb-driver skill that shows SRV mongoClusters URIs and the 10260 port guidance, and mark the legacy cosmos.* host/port as a different product.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB) uses Request Units (RUs) for provisioned throughput and also offers a serverless option. Billing is RU/s or serverless; does not use vCore instance classes for the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters use compute tiers (vCore-like tiers such as M30, M40) and storage options; this is a vCore/compute-tier model (not RU-based). Cosmos DB RU/model refers to the RU-based Cosmos DB (RU) offering. The new service (formerly vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB) is billed by compute tier and storage.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters ARM docs (computeProperties.tier example 'M30')
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing and compute model)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the RU billing model used by Cosmos DB (RU-based databaseAccounts). The vCore DocumentDB clusters explicitly use tiers (M30, M40) and compute-based billing.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU-based model docs

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumed RU provisioning, they might attempt to set throughput on a vCore cluster using RU APIs or pick wrong pricing expectations; provisioning and sample guidance would be misleading.
improvements: Add explicit billing model notes to the deployment skill: 'vCore clusters use compute tier (M30 etc.), not RU-based throughput; do not call az cosmosdb create --throughput for these clusters.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API you authenticate with standard MongoDB credentials (username/password). Microsoft Entra ID token-based authentication is not supported by the MongoDB drivers for Cosmos DB; AAD is supported for some Cosmos DB APIs (SQL) but not for the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: vCore-managed DocumentDB supports both native (native user/password) and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication modes on clusters (AuthConfigProperties.allowedModes include 'MicrosoftEntraID' and 'NativeAuth'); drivers can obtain AAD tokens and use the token-callback interface to authenticate (the docs show patterns for DefaultAzureCredential and token callback integration).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters ARM template docs (AuthConfigProperties.allowedModes includes MicrosoftEntraID)
How to build Node.js console app (token-based auth example with @azure/identity)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically the Cosmos DB MongoDB API did not support AAD in the same way, so older guidance states AAD is not supported. The vCore-managed offering adds MicrosoftEntraID support; the model's memory reflected the older limitation.

confusion_sources.title: Older guidance for Cosmos DB's MongoDB API (AAD not supported)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes AAD is not supported, they will implement only username/password flows and miss an opportunity to use managed identities or token-based auth in production. Conversely, if they rely on AAD without enabling cluster auth modes, connection will fail.
improvements: Clarify in documentdb-driver and documentdb-security skills that clusters can enable Microsoft Entra ID and include a short code snippet showing the token-callback pattern with DefaultAzureCredential.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the official mongodb npm package). There is not a separate MongoDB-specific Azure SDK for application data-plane access; the Azure SDKs (e.g., @azure/cosmos) are for the Core/SQL API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct. Applications should use standard MongoDB drivers (mongodb npm package for Node.js) to connect to Azure DocumentDB clusters. The Azure SDK @azure/cosmos targets Core/SQL Cosmos DB and is not for the MongoDB-wire protocol data plane.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Node.js
Build a Node.js console app with Azure DocumentDB (programming-language-js)

confusions.build_risk: None (this is the recommended approach).

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vendor-provided vector algorithms include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Index creation uses the MongoDB createIndex interface with a vector index spec. Example db.transactions.createIndex({ embedding: "vector" }, { vector: { dimensions: 1536, algorithm: "hnsw", distanceMetric: "cosine", m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports IVFFLAT (vector-ivf), HNSW (vector-hnsw) and DiskANN (vector-diskann). The documented way is to create a vector index via the service's index-creation API block (createIndexes/createIndex variants) with 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' or 'vector-*' kind in the index spec; the exact structure uses cosmosSearchOptions or kind: 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' rather than the generic 'vector' key shown in the cold example.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector index examples and 'kind' values)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (create IVF/DiskANN examples)
Build-RAG app guidance (LangChain example showing DiskANN/HNSW/IVF wrappers)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed a plausible Mongo-style createIndex call with an informal 'vector' option. Azure DocumentDB uses a different documented index spec (cosmosSearchOptions / kind vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann) and the $search/cosmosSearch query operator. The model's syntax looked like generic Atlas/experimental syntax.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues the wrong createIndex shape the server will reject the index creation call or create an index that doesn't behave as expected; vector search queries would fail or return no results.
improvements: Add a small code snippet to documentdb-vector-search and documentdb-indexing skills that shows the exact JSON payload or driver command to create each vector index kind (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ textField: "text" })) for full-text. For richer full-text/hybrid search integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search or external engine; or combine text index with vector index client-side.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB exposes a native full-text engine (BM25) via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage; hybrid search is supported natively by combining BM25 search indexes (createSearchIndexes / $search) and vector indexes (cosmosSearch) and fusing results server-side (RRF) or client-side. Using Azure Cognitive Search is NOT required; the service provides an integrated full-text + vector hybrid search.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes + $search, BM25)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector + RRF server-side)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended the community MongoDB text index or an external search engine; DocumentDB provides a preview/GA full-text engine with BM25 and hybrid patterns built-in. The model recalled older or generic approaches.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used only $text and external Cognitive Search, they would miss the integrated BM25 features and the recommended server-side fusion flows and might overcomplicate the sample.
improvements: Update documentdb-full-text-search skill to include a 'quick recipe': enable FullTextSearch, createSearchIndexes example, and server-side RRF example to discourage copying legacy $text-only patterns.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Compatibility depends on account; recent Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB MongoDB API) supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions up to 6.0+; newer clusters may advertise 7.0. Some admin/engine features may be unsupported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports multiple MongoDB wire-protocol/server compatibility versions including 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 depending on cluster/serverVersion; feature coverage is extensive (99.03% operator support) but some server-side admin commands and engine-specific features are managed by the service and may differ. Check the cluster's advertised serverVersion and the compatibility matrix for specific operators.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (compatibility matrix)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (supported MongoDB versions 5.0-8.0)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged and mentioned 6.0+/7.0; the correct current guidance explicitly lists supported versions including 5.0-8.0. The difference is precision rather than a contradictory fact.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a lower maximum version may cause builders to avoid using newer aggregation operators unnecessarily; conversely assuming features from the latest MongoDB release without verifying compatibility may cause runtime errors.
improvements: Add a short 'compatibility' snippet in the documentdb-driver skill showing official supported serverVersion values and a link to the compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows/Linux) but it historically does not fully emulate MongoDB API. For MongoDB-compatible development use the MongoDB server image locally: docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7 and connect on mongodb://localhost:27017. Use the cloud account for vectors/features the emulator doesn't support.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a local DocumentDB gateway Docker image for development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) whose gateway endpoint listens on port 10260; the quickstarts and documentdb-local-deployment skill recommend running that local gateway for feature parity (the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator is limited for Mongo API). Using plain mongo:latest is an option but misses DocumentDB-specific features (vectors, full-text preview).

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB local development loop (DocumentDB local Docker gateway, port 10260)
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (gateway port 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended the generic mongo Docker image; while that works for many basic tests, DocumentDB provides a specific local gateway image (10260) better matched to service features. The model defaulted to the generic Mongo approach.
confusions.build_risk: Using a vanilla mongo:7 local instance will not surface features or behaviors unique to Azure DocumentDB (vector search, full-text preview options, port/ssl differences), which may cause tests to pass locally but fail on the managed cluster.
improvements: Add 'start local gateway' instructions and a one-liner to documentdb-local-deployment skill that shows the ghcr.io/documentdb/container image and port 10260 in the README of the sample repository.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams (watch()) are supported on MongoDB-compatible Cosmos accounts that advertise a supported MongoDB version; may need account version that supports change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB; for multishard change streams you may need to enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' preview feature in the cluster Features settings. The docs include guidance for resuming streams and multi-shard considerations.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (enablement and multi-shard notes)
Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (resume and examples)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams work cluster-wide without enabling multi-shard change-streams on a multishard cluster, they may get incomplete results; verify the feature is enabled for multishard scenarios.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The service-specific MCP server is 'documentdb'. The general Azure MCP Server does not replace the documentdb agent for data-plane MongoDB inspection tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (query/aggregate/index management/explain) and should be used for MongoDB data-plane interactions; the general azure MCP server is control-plane and doesn't provide the same data-plane convenience.

grounding_links.title: documentdb

confusions.build_risk: None; the inventory contains the documentdb MCP server so an agent can use it.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service called DocumentDB that became Azure Cosmos DB. 'DocumentDB' historically refers to the SQL API. Azure Cosmos DB exposes a MongoDB-compatible API. The open-source DocumentDB projects are unrelated.
confusions.grounded_answer: Current docs: the offering formerly named 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' has been renamed to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility); the new Azure DocumentDB is a vCore-managed product distinct from RU-based Cosmos DB accounts. Also, Azure DocumentDB (the new product) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed under MIT and Linux Foundation). The name history is confusing because 'DocumentDB' earlier (2014–2017) was the original DocumentDB that evolved into Cosmos DB; the current 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' is the vCore rebrand of the vCore Mongo offering.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming notes)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated historical DocumentDB/Cosmos naming and omitted that the current vCore-managed offering now uses the Azure DocumentDB name and is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine.
confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion can cause a builder to target the wrong resource type or CLI commands and to mislabel repo artifacts.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming and relation' note in the top of the documentdb-agent-kit README clarifying the lineage and the difference between RU-based Cosmos DB accounts and vCore Azure DocumentDB clusters.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath the MongoDB API is Cosmos DB's proprietary engine implementing the MongoDB wire protocol (a compatibility layer rather than a vanilla mongod). Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers but expect behavioral differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current vCore Azure DocumentDB product is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (not MongoDB's server binary) and in the docs is described as an open-source engine built on PostgreSQL. The key result for application code: continue to use standard MongoDB drivers, but verify specific operator compatibility and behavior against the compatibility matrix — the behavior differences noted in the cold answer (indexing and planner differences) remain relevant, but the engine is not the Cosmos DB proprietary engine as phrased.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (overview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described Cosmos DB's older 'proprietary compatibility layer' idea. The current product runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine; the functional guidance (use MongoDB drivers, expect some differences) is still valid but the engine attribution was incorrect.
confusions.build_risk: Misstating the engine could mislead users about licensing and portability: DocumentDB is open-source and portable, whereas treating it as Cosmos DB proprietary may discourage self-hosting or local gateway use.
improvements: Update public 'about' docs and the agent kit to clearly state the engine (DocumentDB open-source) and what it implies for portability, licensing, and testing.

confusions.question: What exact database and collection names will this sample use and create?
confusions.cold_answer: Database: sample_fintech_02. Collections: transactions (stores transaction docs), embeddings (optional: stores vector embeddings if separated). All sample data and indexes go into sample_fintech_02 only.
confusions.grounded_answer: The run environment explicitly mandates using database sample_fintech_02. The sample's collection names are not specified by the prompt or official docs — using a collection named transactions is a reasonable implementer choice, but not authoritative.

grounding_links.title: Sample run environment (skill_md) states database sample_fintech_02

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer filled in unspecified collection names with reasonable defaults; the run environment only specified the database name.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample code used a different collection name than the verification scripts, the MCP verification calls and queries would target the wrong collection and fail to find the seeded data.
improvements: Explicitly state the collection names (e.g., 'transactions') in the sample prompt or the repository README so the builder and verification tooling use the same names.

confusions.question: What index definitions does this sample need for transaction categorization and the aggregation endpoint?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a text index on free-text fields (description, merchant) via db.transactions.createIndex({ description: 'text', merchant: 'text' }). Create a compound index for aggregation by category and date: db.transactions.createIndex({ category: 1, transactionDate: 1 }). If using vector search, create a vector index on embedding with cosmosSearchOptions.
confusions.grounded_answer: For full-text categorization the recommended DocumentDB approach is either a regular text index (db.createIndex({ field: 'text' })) for simple $text queries, or the new full-text preview engine using createSearchIndexes plus $search for BM25 and advanced analyzers. Aggregations should be supported by an index on { category: 1, transactionDate: 1 } or at least single-field indexes for date and category. Vector indexes must be created with the cosmosSearch / cosmosSearchOptions / vector-kind index spec (vector-hnsw|vector-ivf|vector-diskann) rather than a generic 'vector' createIndex property.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search usage)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector index creation examples)
Manage indexing in Azure DocumentDB (text indexes and createIndex)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed legacy MongoDB text-index usage with the newer createSearchIndexes full-text engine and used an informal vector index shape instead of the documented cosmosSearchOptions form.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong index creation patterns will either create suboptimal indexes (text index when you want BM25 features) or will fail for vector index creation if the API shape is wrong.
improvements: In the documentdb-indexing skill, add an explicit small recipe for this sample: (1) createSearchIndexes for BM25 on description/merchant, (2) create index { category: 1, transactionDate: 1 }, (3) create a vector index using the documented cosmosSearchOptions if embeddings are used.

confusions.question: Exactly how will the Node.js app connect at runtime (command/driver syntax and environment variable)?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the mongodb driver and read connection URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI. Example code shows MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the official mongodb Node.js driver and read the connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI is specified by the run environment). The docs show creating a MongoClient with the connection string and calling client.connect(); modern driver options differ across versions so follow the driver docs, but the high-level pattern (MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI); await client.connect();) is correct.

confusions.build_risk: Minor: sample code using legacy MongoClient options (useUnifiedTopology/useNewUrlParser) should be updated for the driver version pinned in package.json.
improvements: Recommend a driver version in the sample's package.json (e.g., mongodb@5.x or 6.x as appropriate) and update the connection-snippet in README to match the pinned driver options.

confusions.question: What validation/schema or sample documents will the sample write when creating test data?
confusions.cold_answer: Each transaction doc shape the app will write: { _id: ObjectId, amount: Number, currency: 'USD', description: String, merchant: String, transactionDate: ISODate, category: null|String, embedding: [Number] (optional), source: 'bank'|'card'|'import' } — sample loader will insert a few dozen realistic transactions.
confusions.grounded_answer: No authoritative docs specify the sample's exact document shape; the run environment only requires that sample data exist in sample_fintech_02. The proposed shape is reasonable, but not verified by any skill/doc page.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is an implementer assumption to make the sample workable; it is not documented in service docs.
confusions.build_risk: If the seed data shape doesn't match the app's queries (e.g., uses transactionDate vs date field), aggregation endpoints may return incorrect results or no data.
improvements: Sample prompt or repository should include a seed script and exact document schema to remove this ambiguity. Add a small seed.js to the repository that inserts canonical documents.

confusions.question: What prompt engineering and flow will the agent use to categorize a transaction and persist the result?
confusions.cold_answer: Flow: query uncategorized transactions, build a prompt with fixed taxonomy and examples, send to LLM via LangChain, parse single-category response, persist via updateOne, and expose aggregation endpoint that runs an aggregation pipeline grouping by year-month and category.
confusions.grounded_answer: The cold answer describes an appropriate and implementable flow; it is not a prescriptive requirement in docs but is consistent with the LangChain + MongoDB approach and the documentdb-* skills (documentdb-natural-language-querying, documentdb-driver). The specifics (exact prompt, taxonomy, batching, error handling) are implementation choices the builder must make.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer is design guidance rather than a hard service fact; no single doc prescribes the LangChain prompt flow or taxonomy format.
confusions.build_risk: If the agent prompt isn't constrained to the fixed taxonomy and response mapping, the LLM may output labels not in the taxonomy causing mapping/validation bugs when updating documents.
improvements: Add a small 'prompt recipe' example in the sample repo and in the documentdb-natural-language-querying skill that shows how to validate LLM output against a fixed taxonomy before persisting.

information_gaps.title: Fixed taxonomy contents
information_gaps.description: The prompt requires a fixed taxonomy of categories the LLM must choose from, but neither the prompt nor the installed skills provide the canonical list. I looked through the prompt, prompt_review, skill_md, and documentdb skills; no authoritative taxonomy was provided. The builder must choose or be given the category list (e.g., Food, Travel, Utilities, Entertainment, Income, Other).

information_gaps.title: LLM/provider selection and env vars
information_gaps.description: The run environment specifies DOCUMENTDB_URI but not which LLM provider or the names of environment variables for model credentials (e.g., OPENAI_API_KEY, AZURE_OPENAI_KEY). I searched the prompt and skills; no standard env var name is mandated. The builder must decide and document the provider and env vars in .env.example.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset shape & size
information_gaps.description: No skill or doc prescribes the exact seed-document schema, sample rows, or seeding script. The builder needs this to create deterministic tests and to verify the aggregation endpoint. I searched the repo skills and Microsoft docs but found no sample data for this exact sample.

information_gaps.title: Agent invocation mechanism
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for a LangChain agent but leaves unspecified how it's invoked (HTTP endpoint, CLI, scheduled job). No skill or doc mandates a method. The builder must choose and document this in the sample README.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the Azure resource type (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when referring to or deploying vCore-managed clusters.

Connect using the MongoDB driver with the SRV-style connection string provided by the cluster (mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and expect the cluster to use ports starting at 10260 for node endpoints; do NOT use the older mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 host shape for vCore clusters.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: If you plan to use full-text BM25 or hybrid (BM25 + vector) retrieval, enable FullTextSearch on the cluster and create a search index with createSearchIndexes; use the $search stage for BM25 queries and use the cosmosSearch operator for vector queries. Do not rely solely on legacy { field: 'text' } text-indexes if you want BM25 features.
